To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ion beam mismatch between the PTSX source and the focusing quadrupoles can be reduced by increasing the source voltage and by decreasing the injection frequency, and that the number of particles injected into the PTSX device can be minimized by increasing the injection frequency and by decreasing the source voltage.

the injection process for PTSX is optimized by minimizing the mismatch between the beam source and the focusing system, and by minimizing beam particles near the injection electrodes when switching from the fully oscillatory injection waveform to the static trapping waveform.
the PTSX device can be used to simulate the nonlinear dynamics of intense charged-particle beam propagation in periodic focusing quadrupole magnetic lattice transport systems.

developing the PTSX as a tool for understanding the nonlinear dynamics of charged particle beams in quadrupole transport systems.
the optimization of ion injection for the PTSX device, and the results are useful for other similar devices.
understanding the nonlinear dynamics of charged particle beams and the effects of space-charge forces on the propagation of such intense beam systems.

the PTSX device is a useful and versatile tool to study nonlinear beam dynamics in periodic-focusing transport systems.
the ion injection optimization for the PTSX experiment has been successfully achieved.

the injection process is optimized when the beam has a minimum mismatch with the focusing lattice, when the number of particles in the vicinity of injection electrodes is small, and when the injection electrodes have the minimum possible time to reach their static trapping potential.

we have demonstrated the feasibility of using a Paul trap as a source for a one-component plasma experiment.
the PTSX device has been successfully used for the first time to study nonlinear beam dynamics.

it is possible to inject a large number of ions into the central electrodes of the Paul trap, and the injected ion distribution has a high degree of overlap with the desired equilibrium ion distribution.
